source_doubts.quote: The conclusion is then quoted from the companion unitarizability theorem \cite[Theorem~1.1]{OpenAIUnitarizability2026}.
source_doubts.problem: The whole deduction rests on a companion theorem whose statement appears in neither text. For the step to hold, that theorem must give, for every countable nonamenable group, a uniformly bounded non-unitarizable representation with bound 1+epsilon. That is the Dixmier unitarizability problem, which was open in the published literature as far as I know. The corollary therefore cannot be checked from the source and is conditional on the companion paper. The source has the same gap; the rewrite kept it and flagged it.

source_doubts.quote: Apply the companion percolation result \cite[Corollary~1.2]{OpenAIPercolation2026} to \(F\), which is nonamenable by \cref{thm:main}.
source_doubts.problem: Every assertion of the corollary is imported from an unstated companion result: finiteness of the L2 operator norm at p_c, p_c < p_{2->2} <= p_u, infinitely many infinite clusters on (p_c, p_u), and the simultaneous statement on [p_1, p_2]. For arbitrary nonamenable Cayley graphs, p_c < p_u is the Benjamini–Schramm conjecture, open in general as far as I know. Nothing is derived in the source, so the step is unjustified from the text. The source has the same gap; the rewrite kept it and flagged it.

unverified_marks.concern: The companion Theorem 1.1 is cited but not stated, and the rewriter could not consult it. The deduction needs it to hold for every countable nonamenable group with the 1+epsilon bound, which is the open Dixmier problem in the known literature.

The companion Corollary 1.2 is cited but not stated. All conclusions (the bound at p_c, p_c < p_{2->2} <= p_u, non-uniqueness on (p_c, p_u), the simultaneous interval [p_1, p_2]) come from it, and p_c < p_u for general nonamenable Cayley graphs was an open conjecture.
